# A toxicokinetic model for gill processes affecting the uptake of perfluoroalkyl acids by freshwater fish

**Authors:** Zhiji Hu; Jennifer M Sun; Yumin Zhu; Colin P Thackray; Elsie M Sunderland; Fabian C Fischer

**Affiliations:** aHarvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA, Email: zhijihu@seas.harvard.edu | bDepartment of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA, Email: fabian_fischer@brown.edu | cDepartment of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, Rhode Island, USA

## Abstract

Perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) are a well-studied subclass of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Some PFAA bioaccumulate in food webs, and fish consumption is an important vector of human exposure. However, mechanistic studies investigating the relative importance of branchial uptake, tissue partitioning, and renal excretion of PFAA in fish are limited. We developed a mechanistic toxicokinetic (TK) model to examine gill transport as a potential rate-limiting step for PFAA uptake and elimination in fish. The model simulates laboratory conditions and explicitly accounts for transport across the aqueous boundary layer (ABL) at the gill epithelial membrane and co-transport with dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Modeled bioconcentration factors (BCFs) for PFAA containing 4–10 perfluorinated carbons (ηpfc) agreed with laboratory data within one standard deviation of the median. BCFs were most sensitive to by tissue binding (normalized sensitivity coefficients [NSCs] across PFAA: 69% to 102%). Elimination half-lives were sensitive to both tissue binding (57% to 76%) and effective gill permeability (−30% to −96%). ABL thickness at the gill epithelial membrane, rather than the epithelial membrane itself, determines the diffusion barrier for short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 6) and was the most sensitive parameter (97%) affecting elimination half-lives. The gills accounted for 5–47% of tissue-bound PFAA, driven by binding to proteins and partitioning to phospholipids. At an aqueous DOC concentrations of 100 mg L−1, modeled BCFs decreased by up to 22%. Together, these results suggest tissue binding and gill permeability are both important for PFAA bioconcentration, and that uptake and exchange are affected by flow-dependent transport across the ABL at the gill epithelial membrane.

## Environmental significance

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), particularly terminal perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA), are widespread contaminants in freshwater ecosystems that represent an important dietary exposure pathway for humans. This study presents a mechanistic toxicokinetic model that simulates PFAA uptake, tissue partitioning and elimination. The model accounts for differences in tissue binding, gill-mediated transport, and renal elimination. The model suggests that tissue binding provides a reasonable proxy for PFAA bioconcentration, while gill exchange affects the rate at which steady state is approached and therefore controls elimination half-lives. The model can be used to adjust laboratory test setups to represent natural conditions, including flow conditions and dissolved organic carbon levels that regulate transport across the ABL at the gill epithelium.

## Introduction

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are fluorinated organic chemicals that have been produced in large quantities for use in industrial processes and consumer products.1–3 PFAS are widely detected in fish and shellfish, and consumption of contaminated seafood contributes to human and ecological health risks.3,4 Perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) are a well-studied subset of PFAS that include perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) with varying perfluorinated carbon chain lengths (ηpfc).5 PFAA with ηpfc ≥ 6 primarily accumulate in fish blood and highly perfused tissues such as the liver and kidneys.6–8 Prior modeling studies have suggested that gill transport may be a rate-limiting step for PFAA uptake in fish.7 Here, we developed a toxicokinetic (TK) model for freshwater fish with an explicit gill compartment to evaluate the role of gill transport for PFAA uptake, accumulation and elimination.

Most regulatory bioaccumulation studies, including those following OECD Test Guideline 305,9 were designed for neutral hydrophobic chemicals that rapidly permeate fish gills through passive diffusion and accumulate predominantly in lipid-rich adipose tissue.10–13 Bioaccumulation is often approximated using lipid-normalized equilibrium partition coefficients that simulate contaminant bioconcentration.14 In contrast, PFAA are predominantly anionic at environmental pH and exhibit low membrane permeability.15,16 PFAA preferentially associate with albumin and other functional proteins as well as phospholipids,17,18 while showing negligible affinity for storage lipids and more limited affinity to structural proteins.18 Phospholipid and structural proteins are both important for determining tissue-specific accumulation19,20 and whole-body PFAA concentrations.21

Fish gills consist of bilaterally symmetrical filaments that form a countercurrent respiratory chamber. At the epithelial membrane, an unstirred aqueous boundary layer (ABL) develops, where slow laminar flow creates a diffusional barrier to uptake.22,23 The gill epithelium regulates uptake and depuration of gases and ions.24,25 For toxicants, transbranchial absorption is initiated by diffusion across the ABL. ABL thickness determines the resistance to solute permeability at the gill when it is driven by passive diffusion.26,27 Previous models for PFAA uptake across fish gills assumed diffusion resistance or impermeability of specific gill layers mediated by water flow and pH,10–12,28,29 but did not account for the influence of ABL thickness.

Simplified laboratory studies are often used to evaluate the bioconcentration potential of environmental contaminants under representative ecosystem conditions including the effects of varying dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations.30 Co-transport of PFAA with DOC across the ABL may facilitate uptake.31,32 Conversely, binding to DOC may reduce freely dissolved concentrations in water available for biological uptake, potentially lowering observed bioconcentration factors (BCFs).33–35 Lab testing guidelines27 specify DOC concentrations of 2–10 mg L−1, which is more limited than ranges observed in natural aquatic environments that can vary from 0.1 to over 300 mg L−1.36

The main objective of this work was to better understand how gill processes, including ABL thickness and co-transport with DOC, influence uptake and elimination in freshwater fish. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether gill exchange is a rate-limiting step, relative to internal tissue distribution and renal elimination. To do this, we leveraged prior modeling efforts14,29,37–39 and developed a two-compartment TK model (blood and tissues) that explicitly accounts for the gill membrane and boundary layer transport. Compared with previous models, our model retains the gill as the exchange barrier for freely dissolved PFAA between water and blood and resolves its effective permeability from ABL diffusion, gill epithelial membrane permeability, and DOC-mediated transport. Other compartments were simplified to focus on respiratory exchange, tissue distribution, and elimination. We assessed nine PFAA (sulfonic and carboxylic acids with ηpfc = 4 to 10) to investigate chain-length- and functional group-dependent patterns. We compared simulated elimination half-lives and BCFs to laboratory measurements to evaluate model performance8,40,41 and conducted a series of sensitivity analyses to quantify the relative importance of different parameters. This work provides insight into the importance of gill transport processes for PFAA accumulation in freshwater fish.

## Model theory & parameterization

### Model overview

We developed a two-compartment TK model for simulating PFAA bioconcentration in freshwater fish. The model includes separate blood and tissue compartments. The tissue compartment consolidates all extravascular organs and tissues (Fig. 1). Preliminary multicompartment simulations revealed equilibrium partitioning reasonably captures internal tissue distribution. The tissue compartment is assumed to be well-mixed for a small (∼8 g) model fish.42,43 The model specifies respiratory exchange at secondary gill lamellae, where PFAS transfer between water and blood is governed by permeability across the ABL and the gill epithelial membrane.29 Depuration is assumed to occur via renal elimination of the free blood concentration. Refinements relative to previous TK models7 include parameterization of: (1) the permeability of the gill epithelial membrane, (2) ABL diffusion, and (3) effects of DOC binding on both ABL transport and aqueous bioavailability.

The model simulates uptake of a single terminal PFAA at a specified DOC level and accounts for both freely dissolved and DOC-bound forms.44 Precursor uptake and biotransformation are not included in the model parametrization. The model assumes that only freely dissolved PFAA are available for transport across the gill and tissue membranes,17,45 with uptake and distribution governed by permeability along concentration gradients.3 PFAA entering blood and tissues reversibly bind to proteins and partition to lipids and nonlipid organic matter (NLOM), represented here as carbohydrates (glycogen).14 Because sorption and desorption are fast relative to gill exchange and renal elimination, sorption was modeled as a rapid, reversible process governed by partition coefficients and a first-order desorption rate constant.45,46 The total PFAA mass is equal to the sum of free and bound fractions in water, blood, and tissues. The tissue compartment includes the gills, kidneys, liver, muscle, and adipose tissues. Elimination of unbound PFAA from blood occurs via active renal excretion and passive branchial elimination across the gill epithelium.7 Modeled exposure scenarios were limited to uptake from water. Biliary excretion and biotransformation were excluded based on negligible hepatic metabolism and fecal elimination of the tested PFAA in fish.47

### Effective gill transport

Modeled initial uptake of PFAA from water is driven by the concentration gradient between freely dissolved PFAA in water (Cfree,water) and the PFAA-free fish. The diffusive flux across the gill is governed by Pgill, which integrates resistance across both the ABL (PABL, cm s−1) and the gill epithelium (Pmem, cm s−1).2,41

To account for the dual role of DOC, the model incorporates DOC-mediated transport across the ABL and adjusts for the reduced free PFAA concentration in water. PABL is derived from (Dfree + DDOC × KDOC/w × CDOC) × xABL−1, where Dfree and DDOC are the aqueous diffusivities of freely dissolved PFAA and DOC in stagnant water (cm2 s−1), respectively, KDOC/w is the DOC–water partition coefficient for ionized PFAA using organic carbon (OC) as a surrogate (Lwater kgDOC−1), CDOC is the DOC concentration in water (kgDOC Lwater−1), and xABL is ABL thickness (cm). We assumed DOC consists of humic substances at concentrations ranging from 1 × 10−6 g mL−1 to 1 × 10−4 g mL−1.49 In addition to DOC-mediated transport, binding to DOC reduces Cfree,water, which is calculated by Cwater = Cfree,water + Cfree,water × KDOC/w × CDOC,45 where Cwater is the total PFAA concentration in the water (µg cm−3).

The model accounts for chemical diffusion distances across xABL and the gill epithelial membrane (xmem, cm). Simulations were conducted assuming a 45 L flow-through tank representative of typical laboratory exposure conditions. We set xABL depending on the bioaccumulation test setup: under flowing water at 5.8 cm s−1, xABL was set to 0.016 cm; under static conditions, we increased xABL to 0.082 cm.50

### Model parameterization

Modeled PFAA were selected based on data availability for model evaluation,8,40,41 including perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS, ηpfc = 4), perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS, ηpfc = 6), and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS, ηpfc = 8) as well as perfluorohexanoic acid (PFHxA, ηpfc = 5), perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA, ηpfc = 6), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA, ηpfc = 7), perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA, ηpfc = 8), perfluorodecanoic acid (PFDA, ηpfc = 9), and perfluoroundecanoic acid (PFUDA, ηpfc = 10). All modeled PFAA are strong acids with low pKa values (−0.17 to 2.50) and are assumed to be fully ionized at environmental and physiological pH ranges.2,15,51 Partition coefficients (K) reported here therefore describe ionized species and are equivalent to distribution coefficients. Renal elimination rates (ke) were derived from prior studies.7,29 Following the approach of Ng and Hungerbühler,29 missing renal clearance and reabsorption rates were estimated by linear extrapolation over the number of perfluorinated carbons, based on data from Weaver et al.52 Data for PFBS and PFHxA were not available, so we estimated rates from the mean values reported by Lau et al.53 Physicochemical model parameters for PFAA included in this study were derived from in vitro data and are summarized in Tables S2 and S3.

Fish physiological parameters were collected for an 8 g rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Data included tissue and biofluid volumes, protein and lipid contents, and gill membrane morphology. Up to six phases were considered in fish blood and tissues: neutral lipids, phospholipids, functional proteins, structural proteins, nonlipid organic matter, and water. When tissue composition data were unavailable for rainbow trout, values were extrapolated from Labeo rohita, a freshwater fish with comparable physiology.48

The model uses a 13 cm2 surface area for the water-facing membrane of the secondary lamellae (Agill, cm2).29 We estimated the surface area of other fish tissues (Atissue, cm2), including gill (71 cm2), liver (16 cm2), kidney (22 cm2), muscle (34 cm2), and adipose tissue (23 cm2) based on total capillary surface areas to reflect the distribution of PFAA via systemic blood flow.29xmem varies depending on fish species and region of diffusion. Therefore, values representative of gas-exchange regions were used, with an assumed total thickness of 1 to 3 µm.25 Further details on the parameterization of fish physiology are provided in Tables S4 and S5.

### Model fits and performance evaluation

We followed the statistical framework outlined by Martin et al.40 to compare simulated with experimental BCFs. The depuration rate constant (kd, per day) was derived by linear regression of the log-transformed decline in simulated fish concentrations during the depuration phase. The uptake rate constant (ku, L per L per day) was derived by iterative nonlinear regression of time-dependent Cfish during the uptake phase, fitting the kinetic rate equation after correcting for fish growth. To do so, Cfish–time curves were fitted to Cfish(t) = a × exp(−kd × t) during the depuration period and blobs/8450/13555787/4a5aa3c363f3/d6em00160b-t6.jpgcdnNEVER_LOAD during the uptake period, where blobs/8450/13555787/4ca3b04abf28/d6em00160b-t7.jpgcdnNEVER_LOAD is the mean concentration of PFAA in water. To represent different laboratory conditions, two exposure scenarios were simulated: (i) a standard laboratory test setting, in which a single initial PFAA spike was added to the water, accounting for depletion of Cfree,water over time due to sorption to DOC and uptake into the fish; and (ii) a modified test setting for flow-through water systems that mimics natural freshwater systems, in which Cfree,water was assumed to remain constant. Elimination half-lives were calculated as ln(2)/kd. Apparent BCFs were determined from laboratory simulations as ku/kd given the standard laboratory test setting. Aqueous-exposure BCFs (BCFaq.) were assumed equal to the apparent BCF at steady state37,54,55 and calculated as the ratio of total modeled PFAA concentration in fish to that in water (Cfish/Cwater) at the end of the 28-day uptake period given the modified laboratory test setting. We examined the influence of variability in experimental partition coefficients by performing Monte Carlo simulations (n = 10 000 iterations), sampling each coefficient from its distribution. Following Fischer et al.,56 values reported by multiple studies were combined by inverse-variance-weighted averaging, and log10-transformed coefficients were represented by normal distributions with means and standard deviations summarized in Tables S2 and S3.

Model performance was evaluated by comparing simulated BCFs to experimental data reported by Burkhard et al.8 and Martin et al.40 For each PFAA, we extracted the median and standard deviation of measured BCFs across relevant exposure conditions. In addition, we assessed model sensitivity to parameter uncertainty using normalized sensitivity coefficients (NSCs, %), calculated as NSC = (Δr/r) × (p/Δp) × 100, where r represents the modeled output (i.e., BCF or elimination half-life), and p the parameter perturbed by 1%. An NSC > 100% indicates that a relative change in model input results in a greater relative change in model output.57

We evaluated the influence of parameters involved in three key processes: (1) mass transfer from water to blood, (2) blood–tissue distribution, and (3) elimination from blood, on predicted BCF and elimination half-lives. All simulations were performed in R (version 4.4.1) using the deSolve package (version 1.40).58

## Results & discussion

### Model evaluation

Modeled log10 BCFs for nine PFAA largely reproduced empirical values for freshwater fish within one log10 unit from literature-reported medians (Fig. 2). All simulations reached steady state by day 28, with <3% change in total fish concentrations over the final 48 hours of the uptake phase. Steady-state BCFsaq estimated under the modified laboratory test setting (i.e., constant PFAA influx) increased across PFAA, with values of 0.92 ± 0.05 (95% CI = 0.83–1.0) for PFBS, 1.1 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 0.99–1.1) for PFHxA, 1.7 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 1.6–1.7) for PFHpA, 1.9 ± 0.05 (95% CI = 1.8–2.0) for PFOA, 2.2 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 2.1–2.2) for PFNA, 2.4 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 2.3–2.4) for PFHxS, 2.7 ± 0.06 (95% CI = 2.5–2.8) for PFOS, 2.7 ± 0.06 (95% CI = 2.5–2.8) for PFDA, and 2.8 ± 0.03 (95% CI = 2.7–2.9) for PFUDA.

Apparent BCFs were well captured for PFBS (1.3 ± 0.02 with 95% CI = 1.3–1.4 vs. 1.1 ± 0.49), PFOA (2.0 ± 0.04 with 95% CI = 1.9–2.0 vs. 1.4 ± 0.61), PFOS (2.8 ± 0.10 with 95% CI = 2.6–3.0 vs. 3.0 ± 0.66), and PFNA (2.2 ± 0.03 with 95% CI = 2.2–2.3 vs. 2.8 ± 0.51), while PFDA (2.8 ± 0.10 with 95% CI = 2.6–3.0 vs. 3.8 ± 0.48) and PFUDA (3.2 ± 0.11 with 95% CI = 3.0–3.4 vs. 3.6 ± 0.31) were moderately underestimated. PFHxA (1.4 ± 0.02 with 95% CI = 1.4–1.4 vs. 0.98 ± 0.30), PFHpA (1.8 ± 0.04 with 95% CI = 1.7–1.9 vs. 1.3), and PFHxS (2.4 ± 0.04 with 95% CI = 2.4–2.5 vs. 2.1 ± 0.25) were on the higher end of the literature values. Discrepancies between modeled and experimental values may result from simplified assumptions in the model, including respiratory-only uptake and the absence of fecal elimination, which could bias accumulation estimates upward and downward for short- and long-chain PFAA, respectively. Despite these limitations, the model captured the chain length-dependent increase in bioaccumulation potential observed across both apparent BCF and BCFaq profiles.8

Modeled water concentrations remained stable during the 12-day uptake phase and closely matched measured values for all PFAA as reported by Martin et al. (Fig. S2).40 Simulated blood concentrations were approximately two-fold higher than measured values for PFHxS (sim. mean on day 12: 0.20 vs. exp. mean on day 12: 0.089 µg mL−1) and PFOA (0.063 vs. 0.040 µg mL−1), but substantially underestimated PFOS (0.029 vs. 1.2 µg mL−1), PFDA (0.053 vs. 1.5 µg mL−1), and PFUDA (0.025 vs. 2.9 µg mL−1), corresponding to 41-, 28-, and 110-fold discrepancies, respectively. Long-chain PFAA (ηpfc ≥ 8) typically show higher bioaccumulation than ηpfc < 8 PFAA. These discrepancies appear to reflect the measured blood concentrations rather than the model structure. Within the experimental dataset, blood concentrations of PFOS, PFDA, and PFUDA exceed those of PFOA by 30- to 70-fold at comparable exposure concentrations, a gap larger than expected given that these compounds partition preferentially into phospholipid- and protein-rich tissues rather than remaining in blood. The resulting rank order of blood concentrations simulated by the TK model (PFHxS > PFOA > PFDA > PFOS > PFUDA) was instead consistent with more recent in vivo studies that reported higher blood burdens of PFHxS and PFOA compared to PFOS, irrespective of exposure route.59,60

### Sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analyses indicate that modeled whole-body BCFs are primarily controlled by tissue–water partitioning, whereas gill exchange has a strong influence on elimination half-lives (Fig. 3). For BCFs (Fig. 3A), normalized sensitivity coefficients (NSCs) were highest for tissue binding (Ktissue/w), ranging from 69% for PFHxS (ηpfc = 6) to 102% for PFUDA (ηpfc = 10). This indicates that a 2-fold increase in Ktissue/w leads to a 69–102% increase in predicted BCFs. In contrast, BCFs were only moderately sensitive to gill permeability (Pgill), with NSCs up to 23% for PFUDA, but ≤10% for ηpfc ≤ 7 PFAA. Renal elimination (ke) had a minor influence on BCFs for short-chain PFAA (e.g., −2.4% for PFBS, −2.4% for PFHxA), and was negligible for compounds with ηpfc ≥ 7, with NSCs around zero. These patterns align with other fish TK models, where BCF increases as renal elimination slows while gill uptake remains unchanged. Stronger tissue binding slows redistribution and clearance, elevating the steady-state uptake-to-loss ratio.13 Experimental data similarly show that long-chain PFAS preferentially accumulate in tissues rich in phospholipids and proteins.19,20,61 These results suggest that gill uptake and tissue retention are more important drivers of experimental bioconcentration factors over 28-day uptake and depuration periods rather than renal clearance for the PFAA evaluated in this study.7

Elimination half-lives were primarily governed by gill exchange and tissue binding, with sensitivity patterns varying by chain length (Fig. 3B). NSCs for gill permeability (Pgill) ranged from −30% for PFDA (ηpfc = 9) to −96% for PFBS (ηpfc = 4), underscoring the important role of gill exchange in PFAA elimination. NSCs for tissue binding (Ktissue/w) were uniformly positive, ranging from 57% (PFDA) to 76% (PFOS). Rapid branchial exchange lowered the blood concentration and steepened the tissue-to-blood gradient, driving net redistribution of PFAA out of tissues. Stronger tissue binding opposed this by retaining PFAA in tissue. Elimination half-lives were therefore dominated by gill exchange for the shorter-chain PFAA and by tissue binding for long-chain PFAA (ηpfc ≥ 7). We found minimal influence of renal elimination on elimination half-lives for long-chain PFAA. This result aligns with trout analyses showing that adding a renal-elimination term improves agreement mainly for short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 7). Respiratory (gill) elimination tends to be orders of magnitude greater than renal elimination for long-chain PFAA (ηpfc ≥ 7),7 which is similar to neutral persistent organic pollutants (POPs).7

To identify processes controlling Pgill, we analyzed the sensitivity of the gill model subcomponents. The ABL emerged as the dominant diffusional barrier. NSCs for ABL thickness (xABL) ranged from −2.1% for PFOA to −23% for PFUDA with respect to BCFs, and from +31% (PFDA) to +97% (PFBS) for half-lives. In contrast, gill membrane diffusion (Dmem), binding to gill membranes (Kmem/w), and gill membrane thickness (xmem) mostly had NSCs below ±0.01%. These results indicate that for aqueous exposures resistance across the ABL at the gill surface, not the epithelial membrane itself, may be the dominant diffusional barrier. Sensitivity of aqueous diffusion of free PFAA was almost 100% responsible for Pgill, suggesting that diffusion of free PFAA across the ABL is likely the rate-limiting step for overall mass transport across the gills.

Under the tested conditions, DOC-mediated transport across the ABL had a minor influence on modeled results. NSCs for PFAA partitioning to DOC (KDOC/w) and DOC concentrations in laboratory water (CDOC) were generally between −0.001% and −0.7% for BCFs, and up to −1.0% for half-lives (PFUDA). These effects were measurable only for long-chain PFAA and remained small compared to ABL diffusion and tissue binding. Our results agree with earlier models for hydrophobic organic contaminants, where DOC sorption reduces freely dissolved contaminant concentrations and affects overall mass transport when hydrophobicity and DOC levels are both high.31,32

### Influence of environmental factors on BCFs

To assess changes in BCFs under environmentally relevant conditions, we varied each parameter individually, holding all others constant. Model simulations revealed that changes in ABL thickness following changes in water flow and high aqueous DOC concentration can influence PFAA BCFs. DOC was predicted to have minimal impact in typical freshwater environments (Tables S6 and S7). Comparing flow-through conditions, which yielded an ABL thickness of 0.016 cm, to static conditions with an ABL of 0.082 cm,50 median BCFs decreased by <0.01–26%, with the largest effects observed for short-chain PFAA (Tables S6 and S7). Similar findings have been reported for highly hydrophobic compounds, where ABL diffusion in internal compartments such as the gastrointestinal tract can limit uptake.62

DOC-related parameters exhibited low sensitivity overall (NSC < ±0.1%), yet BCFs decreased by up to 22% at elevated DOC concentrations (CDOC = 1 × 10−4 g mL−1). Reductions in BCFs correlated with the log KOC of the compounds (1.51–4.20). This result is consistent with previous models that predicted lower uptake of superhydrophobic compounds due to reductions in freely dissolved, bioavailable concentrations in the water phase.27 Large reductions in BCFs are not expected under typical ranges of environmental DOC levels.49,63 For PFAA with log KOC < 3, BCFs changed by less than 2%. Under the modified laboratory test setting, PFUDA (log KOC = 4.20) decreased by only 12%, likely due to constant influx sustaining the free aqueous concentration and enhancing DOC-mediated transport. These findings suggest that using a standard laboratory setting in BCF tests (i.e., single PFAA spike) could underestimate the bioconcentration potential of long-chain PFAA with high affinity for organic matter in natural water sources (i.e., constant PFAA influx) with high DOC content (e.g., swamp waters >30 mg L−1).63

### Distribution of PFAA among fish tissues

Across the seven tissues in the model, blood contained the largest mass fraction of PFAA but not the highest concentration (Fig. S2). Compartments such as the gills and kidneys exceeded blood concentrations but accounted for lower total mass due to their smaller volumes. These rankings are not directly comparable with reported field concentrations, which are usually measured in plasma or serum and account for 40–50% of whole blood in fish.64 Modeled whole-blood values reported here are correspondingly lower. Tissue-to-blood ratios above one for several PFAA are consistent with aqueous-exposure distribution studies.65 Because tissue partitioning was identified as one of the primary drivers of BCFs and elimination half-lives, we further examined the distribution of PFAA across individual fish tissues. We modeled the PFAA distribution across six tissues following aqueous exposures of 28 days in the gills, liver, kidneys, muscle, adipose, and rest-of-body (Fig. 4). Muscle accounted for the largest fraction of total PFAA body burden (14–84%) due to its large volume (47% of body mass), despite comparatively lower concentrations. Highest concentrations were simulated in the kidneys, followed by the gills and liver, with lower levels in adipose, muscle, and the “rest” compartment. Tissue mass fractions followed the order: muscle > gills > kidneys > liver > adipose > rest. Concentrations were highest in the kidneys and gills, intermediate in liver and adipose, and lowest in muscle and “rest” of the body. PFUDA deviated from this pattern, exhibiting both a high muscle burden and elevated adipose concentrations.

For short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 7), kidney concentrations were highest, followed by the gills and liver. Concentrations in the gills were 1.2–1.3-fold higher than in the liver and 25–50-fold higher than in muscle. For example, PFHxS concentrations in the gills were 1.2× higher than the liver, 1.2× lower than in kidney, and over 60× higher than in muscle. Sub-compartment modeling indicated that PFAA predominantly bind to functional proteins (73–99% of total PFAA in gills), followed by structural proteins (0.48–14%) and phospholipids (0.28–12%) (Fig. S3). This distribution pattern likely reflects the high total protein content (20%) of gills, including functional (4.1%) and structural proteins (16%), as well as phospholipids (0.23%),48 in combination with binding affinities of PFAA to functional proteins (log KFP/W = 3.3–4.9), structural proteins (log KSP/W = 0.64–3.6), and phospholipids (log KPL/W = 2.3–5.2). These results suggest that binding to proteins and phospholipids in the gills is a major driver of PFAA bioaccumulation in fish. This is particularly relevant for compounds with shorter perfluorinated chain lengths (ηpfc < 7), which, in this case study, deposited over 20% of the total body burden in the gills.

### Implications for laboratory and field bioaccumulation studies

Our findings have several implications for interpreting PFAS bioaccumulation data and for improving food-web modeling frameworks. For long-chain PFAA (ηpfc > 7), tissue binding dominated BCFs, indicating that bioconcentration is primarily governed by tissue composition, particularly protein and phospholipid content. Given equal aqueous PFAA exposures, BCF values are likely to be more sensitive to interspecies differences in tissue composition across habitats and evolutionary branches relative to hydrodynamic conditions. In contrast, short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 7) exhibited greater sensitivity to gill permeability, specifically transport across the ABL, indicating that processes affecting ABL thickness, such as water flow, mixing, and ventilation rates, may substantially influence uptake and depuration. This mechanistic distinction likely explains the higher variability observed in laboratory BCF measurements for short-chain PFAS8 and underscores the importance of standardizing turbulence and flow conditions across experimental systems.

Classical food-web models that represent bioaccumulation as an equilibrium partitioning process are likely to capture long-chain PFAS behavior when tissue binding is parameterized for protein- and phospholipid-rich tissues rather than neutral storage lipids alone.19 However, such models are insufficient for short-chain PFAS (ηpfc < 7) because uptake is strongly controlled by gill-mediated transport and hydrodynamic conditions. Accumulation of short-chain PFAA may be lower in environmental settings with low water movement and thick ABLs, such as lentic systems or sheltered bays compared to well-mixed rivers or coastal waters, whereas long-chain PFAS bioaccumulation remains largely insensitive to flow and is instead driven mainly by tissue composition.

Environmental drivers of PFAA bioaccumulation have historically received limited attention beyond pH effects.16 The TK model developed here highlights tissue binding and gill transport as important rate-limiting processes governing PFAS uptake and depuration, with the relative importance of each strongly dependent on fluorinated carbon chain length. Results show that effective gill permeability is largely controlled by ABL diffusion of freely dissolved and DOC-bound PFAA in waters rich in organic matter, emphasizing the need to account for both species-specific tissue composition and aqueous conditions such as flow regime and DOC concentrations. For example, marine species exhibit thinner blood–water diffusion distances at secondary lamellae than freshwater species such as perch,66 which may contribute to differences in uptake efficiency. Future models could incorporate the “leaky” nature of gill epithelia, including the role of tight junctions and associated proteins, which remain understudied.67

The model does not account for feedback between PFAS exposure and tissue composition, which may further modify bioaccumulation. Recent work showed that PFOA exposure can upregulate specific phospholipid subclasses in zebrafish liver,68 potentially increasing hepatic binding capacity for PFAA. Although PBTK models typically assume homogeneous tissue compartments,42,43 distribution within a tissue can be heterogeneous, reflecting regional differences in perfusion, membrane permeability, and binding.69–72 Resolving tissues at finer spatial resolution could improve the model for larger fish, where internal distribution is more likely to limit BCFs. In addition, large uncertainty in DOC binding, often parameterized as a function of KOW with confidence intervals spanning orders of magnitude, remains a key limitation for predicting PFAS uptake in DOC-rich systems.73 We used humic substances as a proxy for DOC,49 reflecting the allochthonous organic matter that dominates typical freshwater systems. However, DOC composition varies across systems, and autochthonous organic matter from phytoplankton, macrophytes, and microbial production is also important.74 Extending the model to these systems will require new data on PFAA partition coefficients for diverse types of DOC. Finally, conventional regulatory bioconcentration tests may fail to capture environmentally relevant exposure dynamics or critical life stages. The model simulates respiratory uptake of individual PFAA. Future extensions could add other exposure routes, such as dietary uptake, which becomes more important for longer-chain PFAA, as indicated in previous work.7 The model developed in this study only simulates exposure to terminal PFAA, but precursors such as perfluoroalkyl sulfonamides (FASA) can biotransform to terminal PFSA75 and, where present, can be important determinants of tissue concentrations. Representing precursor uptake would require additional data on biotransformation in the liver and gut and addition of such processes to the model. Mechanistic models such as the one presented here can help guide experimental design and improve alignment between laboratory bioaccumulation tests and real-world aqueous and biological conditions across ecosystems by explicitly incorporating hydrodynamics, aqueous conditions, and tissue composition.
